text:
Value is relative. What some find something valuable some others don't. We're just being human. As for me, I am all for ray tracing since illumination in a game can make it feel more immersive, grant gravitas, make it look more realistic. Take for example driving in GTA V. Even the best of current GPU's cannot render a mirror image on the rearview mirror  because it takes a lot of GPU/CPU resources. And trust me, driving around WITHOUT being able to see what lies behind affects immersion negatively. Just google how many gamers are baffled why mirrors in GTA do not reflect images in real time, well, with ray tracing this would be possible. 

So it is not only about performance, it's about new technologies, we should support the industry going forward, if not with our pockets at least with our attitudes and being more positive about the future.

This is exactly what happens when there's no competition at the high end. Nvidia is now free to milk people for every last penny, simple as that. I guarantee you, if AMD had a true high end competitor to these cards, you wouldn't have a $1,200 2080 Ti FE card, it'd be $700 and Nvidia would be fine.  Instead we get what amounts to essentially zero performance gain for the same price and if I want something faster than my 1080 Ti, I get to drop $500 more than I paid for it. I'll skipping this nonsense and praying that one day AMD can get their sh*t together and compete on the high-end again. 

Kudos to Nvidia though, they've reached a point where we now see the fruit of their way over priced OG Titan card.  At the time they went to great lengths to convince people that it was a boutique card, it wasn't really meant for gaming, it just happened to be good at it. text:
The price is not ridiculous, it's the name that is. Simply imagine that the naming of these cards are like this:

For $1.000: Titan Xv (for example) - currently 2080Ti - previously Titan X
For $700: 2080Ti  - currently 2080 - previously 1080Ti
For $500: 2080 - currently 2070 - previously 1080
For $400: 2070 - supposedly 2060 - previously 1070

You are buying Pascal performance at Pascal prices again but with GDDR6 (that only makes a difference in bandwith at 4K) and 12nm (which is basically a 16nm+ process).
Nvidia does not NEED to make new GPU's this year to begin with, not even next year, they just needed a new excuse to sell Pascal again. If you really think about it, it actually feels like if they had released NOTHING at all.

So in short: no new GPU's for the coming years, buy Pascal/Polaris now and concentrate on new CPU releases.

The price of the 20 series is a joke, I can't believe people actually paid the ludicrous prices for these. It would have been a good normal launch if they charged $700 for the 2080 ti, $550 for the 2080, and reduced the 1080 ti to $500.

The cards show a decent improvement compared to the previous gen (for the same model), but Nvidia is charging a ludicrous premium for having the RTX technology. The problem is that Nvidia knows that having ray tracing enabled is going to destroy the performance of the cards and nobody is going to want to use it until at least one or two more generations. Because of this, Nvidia is probably not allowing game developers to enable ray tracing on launch because it will get bad reviews and they want to wait until enough people shell out a ton of money for this new technology so they can be disappointed later. The cards are good at rasterisation, but that increase in performance alone is not worth the massive increase in price.

I think ray tracing will be a great technology and make games look much better, but I just don't think the performance will be there in the first gen of GPUs. I think most people will opt to turn the features off and play at higher resolutions and frame rates.

I also think Nvidia chose to launch these cards at such a ridiculously high price because they have a massive overstock of 10 series cards because they made too many on the hopes that they would sell to miners, but that fell through. They need to sell off the rest of the 10 series and don't want to make these cards competitive or else they will have to reduce the price of the 10 series or nobody would buy them.

text:
Mate, I get the "not recommended" seal of disapproval you put on these cards. For now. But criticizing and even mocking ray-tracing is short-sighted and uninformative. There's a good reason Nvidia made such a fuzz about this tech: it is a game changer, quite literally. You might not see it now, but being a tech reviewer well… you should.
RTX reminds me a lot of when Nvidia introduced the GeForce 256, the "world's first GPU". The unprecedented T&L Engine made little to help games available then. And it was rather slow for the  initial wave of games that came out with early support.
You see, that is usually the case when a visionary company introduces a paradigm shift. It's a chicken and egg situation that demands a period of growth. We're kinda seeing something similar with VR right now.
My point is: it's ok for the average consumer to be skeptical and even cynical. But tech influencers should be supporting this kind of drastic evolution, even when it's not an instant buy. Which it almost never is with new tech.
Maybe you should have a look at Digital Foundry's take on the subject. Those guys are truly helping move the industry forward.

Hey Vsauce, Blur here. But what are, drivers? They are the framework that the architecture of your graphics processing unit uses to communicate with an API. *=Taken with RTX on.

text:
Hmm.. some wildly different conclusions made in this video compared to a lot of other reputable reviewers.  We're looking at a 25% performance bump for a 75% increase in cost.  

And let's call out the premium on the pricing for these cards for what it is:  Nvidia is essentially applying a surcharge to fund R&D for ray tracing.  Now, any time you buy a technical product, you're helping to fund R&D for future products.  But I've never seen a company do what Nvidia is doing here, where they're essentially giving you a tiny, worthless taste of a technology that's still probably 5-7 years from usefulness and charging you a $200-400 premium for the "future".

I've  held off on getting a new gpu until reviews came out on the RTX line and I will absolutely not be purchasing an RTX card. The sad thing is that I'm Nividia's target buyer for the 2080 ti. I have plenty of disposable income, but i won't buy something that's so transparently overpriced for what it offers.

text: Simply because most developers out there are used to older tech in software terms and NVidia - who were pushing DX11 for so long - are a prime reason for it. As it is a very similar situation with DX12. Shadow of the Tomb Raider is basically the first proper DX12 title and it's coming 3 years after the launch of the API. Vulkan is (roughly speaking) Open GL's version of DX12. AMD's GCN cards have had great support for those since day one, but most developers wouldn't jump on that bandwagon, cause Nvidia owned most of the market. Now that RTX cards can do what AMD cards can, things will change though.

text:
Hi Steve, thanks for the benchmarks, but as with your last video you're still not fully understanding the concept and future power of raytracing and DLSS, together with the procedure it involves for it to yield s full potential.

You cannot expect all games to run off a brand new hardware platform that no game development studios have had time to implement into their games. 

Cart before the horse, as they say. 

You can however see a boost in performance of the 2080 over the 1080 ti when the code is even remotely optimized, as with Wolfenstein II in your tests This is only the start of what performance gains the RTX will be capable of.

Once game devs get their hands on the cards in a few weeks, there will also not suddenly be a rush of optimized games for you to run more benchmarks on, as you will see the same results. 

Tech like this does not simply just happen at the flick of a switch. It's a long procedure. 

The development software teams such as UE4 and Unity (or in-house software like frostbite etc) need to first code this new architecture into their game engines, BEFORE game devs can make use of it and only THEN implement it into their game titles.  Even though they say Frostbite has RTX, i assure you they haven't had nearly enough time to optimize it and you will see many patches coming in the near future for exactly this.

The other very important factor behind the RTX architecture is the fact that it has 3 cores which when implemented and utilized properly will leave the 1080 in its dust. All your benchmarked games aren't making use of Tensor Core and its DLSS yet a they are still running off TSAA, which is still putting massive burden off the SM core of the RTX because it's simple not optimized to do anything else. Once done or DLSS is coded into more games, will you see improved results.

Then there is the matter of drivers. We don't even have DXR yet, so basically all these games are running off rasterization and an unoptimized RT for SotTR.

While you are a hardware benching pro, you don't seem to have much knowledge of what goes on behind the scenes, when making a game from an artist or coders point of view. Making the games you benchmark, look as good as they currently do using rasterization is nothing more than a massive pain in the ass. These artists are insanely talented to achieve what you see with such an old and limited technology. It's temperamental, tedious and takes months of late nights, hacking something together, to try recreate real life lighting, while knowing fully well you'll never achieve it. 

With RT this all becomes MUCH easier, as the computer now does all that heavy lifting for you as an artist, while achieving lighting and texture result that you would never be able to with rasterization. Now you are free to be an artist and not a graphic hacker. 

What does this mean? 

Well less time spent on unnecessary game development, which could either be spent elsewhere. You guys are so focused on benchmarks and frame rates that you completely negate the fact that they are just a small part of what goes into a quality gaming experience. 

If the music in a game is crap, or the AI sucks, the story is bad or networking doesn't work, you hate the game far more than if it runs a few FPS slower. Perfect example is when WOW servers are down during expansion releases. At that point no one cares for frame rates, because with now servers, there are 0 frame to be had. You just don't realize that these other elements exists because they are usually done so well in AAA games. They do however take an enormous amount of time, skills and money to get to this level of excellence, much like the graphical department.

Now with the help of RT and AI these studios or indies, have to put much less effort into their graphics, allowing them to allocate either time or money into making these other elements even better or releasing content faster.. 

Quicker turnover time for their game means more content DLCs/expansions or more time and budget spent on the multitude of other factors that make up a quality game, as mentioned above.

There is more to making a game than just frame rates and so many benchmarks. 

As an ex-3d artist and hobbyist indie game dev, i promise that making even the most basic game is no simple task and the reason why so many “fail”. The graphical part with rasterization is a massive time sink, leaving no time or money left to do everything else. RTX now has the potential to be a massive assistance in this. With this many more indies with less budget than AAA studio have a higher chance to finish a really good looking game.

This is why Jensen is so excited. He see the future potential. Do yourself a favor and go onto a 3D artist forum. You won't see a single complaint, as they know the true potential the RTX brings. 

Editing software such as Resolve as also going to be using the AI core in their interface.

So yes benchmark away, as i know it's your job, and you are the best at it, i always enjoy your videos, I'm just asking to please first understand the process that is required to get RTX into the mainstream, that its not ONLY about the graphical frame rates and what goes on behind the scene for game devs and how they benefit from RTX as a whole, before jumping to any more uninformed conclusions.

Devs will have to support both rasterization and RT for probably the next two years as many people will still want to play their games using a 1080. But once RTX becomes more of a household item, devs with have no love lost for rasterization and will happily never want to see it again, buy which time 1080s will become doorstops.

However, at this point is much better to buy a 1080 ti for current titles, no argument there. But the current benchmarks here will change very quickly over then next 6 to 12 months once all games and drivers are properly optimized for RTX. 

This is a sumamry of my article https://www.fullexposure.photography/nvidia-turing-rtx-raytracing-explained/ as its important to see it form this point of view, when you have never attempted making any form of game before.

Thanks

text:
Radu, I like how you took what I said and quoted it out of context, a great way to make a straw man argument!!! Funnily enough, I followed that up by saying "based on the available statistics, less than 10%". 

Guess what? That makes you part of that small minority of less than 10%!! In fact, it makes you part of the ~4% of people who are currently running 1440p. Would you like a cookie? Or do you just want to be enraged for the sake of being enraged? 

That being said, your particular situation DOES NOT change the fact that about 90% of PC gamers are still running 1080p or less. Roughly 30% of people are running 1680 x 1050, or less, and about 60% of people are running 1080p... Leaving only ~10% running 1440p or greater. Point being, people don't run 1440p-4K because they either can't afford it or simply don't see the point; it's more the former than the latter, regardless of what you want to believe. Otherwise, the GTX 1080 Ti would be used by more than 1.45% of people, the GTX 1080 would be used by more than 2.72%, the GTX 1070 would be used by more than 4%, and the 1070 Ti would be used by more than 0.75%. It's actually funny, there are over 2x the number of people running a GTX 750 Ti as there are a GTX 1080 Ti - why do you think that is? Beyond that, there are 4x the amount of people running a GTX 1050 compared to those running a GTX 1080 - are they all waiting for 4K capable GPUs? 

How can you say the performance is the same? The RTX 2080 is the same as the 1080 Ti in some games, for sure, that's undeniable. BUT, the RTX 2080 Ti is way more powerful than literally anything else we have access to right now, including the $2999 Titan V! And of course it's going to be more expensive than other x/x80 Ti cards, ESPECIALLY at launch. No other x/x80 Ti card has ever released at the same time as the x/x80 and x/x70 - ever. The GTX 1080 had a $699 MSRP and was heavily marked up on release - I paid $779 for mine and a buddy paid something like $850 (like an idiot) for some air-cooled EVGA model. IF the GTX 1080 Ti released at the same time, it probably would have had an MSRP of $899-$999 and likely would have been selling for ~$1100 for the first month or two - especially going into the holiday season when everything gets marked up so sales look better. 

When have I said, even once, that it's a good idea to buy an RTX 2080? Not once. I didn't say that about the RTX 2080 Ti, either. However, if a person is aiming for flawless 4K gaming, then the RTX 2080 Ti is the only option for that right now without spending $3000 on a Titan V only to get worse performance. Either way, people gaming at 4K are basically the 1% of gamers and that's my point. I don't whine when Lamborghini raises the price of the new Huracan, same as I don't whine when the 1% gets fucked elsewhere.

text:
Radu, you are the king of missing points. Get a post box setup and I'll have a crown forged and shipped to you - no joke. 

That "series of comments" was obviously in reply to the notion that we'd all be gaming in 4K if only Nvidia added more CUDA cores to the RTX 2080 Ti - hence the quote right at the top of my reply that was in reference to a previous reply. My point was, even if the RTX 2080 Ti was $600, the vast majority of people still wouldn't buy one because either A.) they cannot afford it, or B.) they cannot justify it due to prior obligations (like having kids, medical issues, a life outside of gaming, etc). I mean, most people are running builds that cost about the same as a single 1080 ti. When it comes down to what people type into search engines, terms related to "budget" and "cheap" are the most common - why is that? 

It's not that people are necessarily waiting for cards to come down in price... It's that these trends have ALWAYS been consistent - always. Go check it out the Steam Hardware Survey for yourself, if you haven't already. 

I'll put it this way, there are roughly 6x the people running a GTX 1050 Ti as there are running a GTX 1080 Ti - it's not because they're waiting for prices to come down on high-end cards. As for the RX 580, it's less than 0.5%, same with the vega cards and the fury / fury x - but that's only because the RX 580 was so insanely hard to buy (for a reasonable price) up until recently. 

If you believe otherwise, you're living in a non-existent utopia where the majority of people are not living paycheck to paycheck and barely scratching by - which in reality they are, regardless of what people post online. And in all honesty, arguing otherwise kiiiind of makes you seem like a bit of a pretentious douchebag, but that's just my opinion. 

Also, you misunderstood. I didn't say you were in the top 4%. I said you are in a group of roughly 4% of PC gamers who run 1440p. In comparison, only 1.3% of people run 4K monitors; aka, the *one percent*. My bad for not explaining better. 

Everything else you've said is effectively irrelevant bullshit. I've never said these cards are good value - because they're not. That doesn't change the fact that the RTX 2080 Ti shows really solid 4K performance in comparison to the 1080 Ti. There's only one test that currently exists, but it does show the RTX 2080 Ti beating the Titan V in a benchmark - but that's not necessarily my point. My point is, to get solid 60fps 4K performance BEFORE the RTX 2080 Ti, you pretty much needed a Titan V. Now, you don't, and with an RTX 2080 Ti you'll potentially get better gaming performance across the board, eventually. I'm not talking about professional workloads; obviously those people are going to buy a Titan V or something even more specialized.

I am surprised, but still not impressed. It is, when using DX11/OpenGL, equivalent to a tier shift which is an acceptable generation leap, but... there are still a few highly disappointing points. This is two generations not one; I won't hold this against them too much since AMD didn't do much better with Vega, but that isn't a bar you should be aiming for. Also, a tier shift hardly counts when you raise prices by a tier. 

I am glad that Nvida has proper support for Vulkan/DX12. Now developers can take the high performance APIs serious which will only benefit gamers. The 2080ti's performance is good enough to justify its existence even if it is a horrible value. And there still is a change that the 2060, 2050, and 2030 will save the generation; if they pull the xx30 series up from the awkward spot of being too good for office work and too weak for gaming, then they could make a compelling lineup in the price range that the masses actually buy.

text:
People still aren't recommending the new gpus, and i agree if you're already running a 1080 or 1080ti. Otherwise, it's definitely a good upgrade.

Here's a few good reasons: 

1) Their price to performance isn't that much worse than pascal, especially not at MSRP.
2) They have more features, like raytracing and dlss, which i can assure you will be used because it's easy to implement
3) They have asynchronous compute support, which makes them even more powerful in games released in the future. They're also newer, so they have better driver support.

Should you upgrade if you already had high-end pascal? Probably not.
If you're wanting to upgrade from a 1060 or 900 series gpu? Definitely go for turing.
